ACT-SC6-P1-Q1.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous. I decoded Figure 1 from the SVG geometry (y=132 is 0 min, y=22 is 50 min, 2.2 px per min) and then rendered it at the authored width=340 and read it by eye; both agree. Additive M at 5 mg/L is an open diamond centred at y=96.8, i.e. 16 min, sitting clearly between the 10-min and 20-min gridlines and above the midpoint. The four options are the four curves' values at 5 mg/L (J 30, K 21, L 9, M 16) and they are 5+ min apart, so no second option survives. Curve identity is triply redundant: bold letters J/K/L/M sit at the right edge beside each line end, the dash patterns differ (solid / long-dash / dotted / dash-dot), and the markers differ (filled circle / open square / filled triangle / open diamond). The finest symbolic distinction in the figure is K's open square (3.6 px) against M's open diamond (4.4 px) at native size; they were still distinguishable in my render, and the dash pattern resolves it independently. One thing a student must do here that the figure does not help with: M is the BOTTOM-but-one curve at 5 mg/L and the TOP curve at 20 mg/L, so tracing back from the right-edge M label crosses K at about 7 mg/L. That is legitimate ACT work, not a defect. Distractors are the standard wrong-curve-same-x set: correct construction, but nothing beyond what every ACT figure item does, hence plausible rather than strong.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q2.pick: Additive J gave its greatest clearing time of the concentrations tested
ACT-SC6-P1-Q2.note: FIGURE READ: readable, but this item contains the second-thinnest discrimination in the batch and it is load-bearing. Experiment 2's concentration (10 mg/L) comes from the passage, not the figure. At 10 mg/L: J 44, K 27, L 8, M 40. J's series is 12/30/44/36/21 so 10 mg/L is a visually obvious peak - the solid line rises steeply to it and falls away on both sides. K (12/21/27/29/30) is still rising past 10 and peaks at 20; L (12/9/8/18/36) is at its MINIMUM at 10 and peaks at 20; both are unmissable. The near-miss is M: 40 at 10, 42 at 15, 41 at 20 - a 2-min margin, which is 4.4 SVG px, about one marker-height. What rescues it is that the 40-min gridline runs exactly through M's 10 mg/L diamond (y=44 is both the gridline and the marker centre) while the 15 mg/L diamond sits visibly above that line. I could see this at the authored 340 px width, so I am not spending a false vote on it - but if this figure is ever re-rendered smaller, or printed at low DPI, M becomes defensible and this item breaks. Flagging for the author: give M a 4-5 min margin at 15 mg/L, or move the M peak further from a gridline, and the item costs nothing to make robust. Distractors strong: four identical sentences differing in one letter, so the option set carries zero information on its own, and each wrong additive fails for a different, real reason (still rising / at its minimum / higher at 15). Second reading of the stem checked: 'its greatest clearing time' could be misread as 'the greatest clearing time of the four additives', but at 10 mg/L J is also the highest of the four, so both readings converge on the same answer - a robustness plus, not an ambiguity.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q3.note: FIGURE READ: this is the thinnest read in the batch and I nearly voted it down. Figure 2 decodes as y=234 is 0 min, y=174 is 50 min, 1.2 px per min, with gridlines ONLY at 0, 25 and 50 - so a 2-min difference is 8% of a gridline interval. Values: J 44 to 17, K 27 to 29, L 8 to 7, M 40 to 36. The key's margin is +2 min = 2.4 px at the authored width; the nearest distractor L's margin is -1 min = 1.2 px, which is about one stroke width of the open bar's outline. At native 340 px I could NOT confidently call the K pair from the thumbnail-scale first look - the two bars read as equal height. I then rendered at 340 and magnified the raster (not the vector), so I was judging only information actually present in the authored-size image: K's open bar top is genuinely above its filled bar top, and L's open bar top is genuinely below its filled bar top. I am voting exclusive true, and the reason is asymmetric rather than comfortable: a student who cannot resolve 2.4 px reads K as a TIE, and a tie is not 'GREATER', so the failure mode is 'no answer', not 'a different answer'. For L to become defensible the student would have to see its open bar as TALLER, and it is drawn shorter - a misread in that direction has nothing in the figure supporting it. So no second option can be defended, which is the test I was asked to apply. But the author should not bank this as-is on the strength of that argument: 2 min against 25-min gridlines is below what the axis supports, and the item survives only because of the direction of the error. Fix is free - make K's stirred bar 34-35 min, or label the Figure 2 axis every 10 min. Distractor quality plausible not strong: J's 27-min drop is a giveaway elimination, and L and M both require the same careful look, so the set is really one near-distractor plus filler. Author called this easy; the arithmetic is easy and the READ is not, so medium.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q4.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous in both figures. The Figure 2 step is the one comparison in that panel nobody can miss - J falls 44 to 17, a 27-min drop of 32 px, while K, L and M differ by 4 min or less. The stem's 'by far more than any other' is therefore honest, and - importantly - it routes the student AROUND the 2.4 px K comparison that Q3 depends on, so this item does not inherit Q3's fragility. Then Figure 1, Additive J at 15 mg/L: filled circle at y=52.8, i.e. 36 min, sitting between the 30 and 40 gridlines and nearer 40. The competing option 42 would plot above the 40-min gridline and J's marker is plainly below it; 29 is a whole gridline away. Best-built item in the batch. Every distractor is the value at 15 mg/L of an additive reachable by a NAMED wrong selection rule applied to Figure 2 - 42 if you take the tallest pair of bars (M), 29 if you take the pair that went up (K), 18 if you take the shortest pair (L). That is a genuine strong set: each wrong answer diagnoses a specific misreading rather than just being a nearby number. Correctly labelled hard - it is the only item requiring both figures.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q5.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous. Additive K's open squares are at 21 min (5 mg/L, y=85.8, just above the 20-min gridline) and 27 min (10 mg/L, y=72.6, between 20 and 30 and nearer 30), and the segment between them is a straight polyline, so 7.5 mg/L interpolates to 24. The read is robust to sloppy reading: even a student who calls the endpoints '20 and 28' lands at 24, and 24 is the only option strictly between the two flanking plotted values, so no second option is defensible. K is also the easiest curve to trace here - it is the only line in the 20-30 band across that interval, with no crossings between 5 and 10 mg/L. Distractors plausible: 21 (the nearer plotted point - the classic 'read the point instead of between the points' error) is a good one, 16 (M at 5 mg/L) is a fair wrong-curve trap, but 12 (the 0 mg/L control) is weak, since nothing in the stem points left. Difficulty medium is right. One batch-level observation to log rather than a defect: 24 is the only numeric option in the whole batch that is NOT a plotted value somewhere in Figure 1 - every other number offered in Q1, Q4 and Q5 sits on some curve. A no-source solver cannot exploit that (they would still need the figure to know WHICH in-between value), but if more interpolation items are authored to this template against option sets of otherwise-plotted values, 'pick the one that is not on any curve' becomes a real cross-item rule. Vary it: give interpolation items at least one distractor that is also off-curve.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q6.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous, with one caveat about what the figure alone tells you. The additive-free level is the single open circle at 0 mg/L, y=105.6 = 12 min, where all four curves converge. Additive L's filled triangles fall to 9 min (y=112.2) and 8 min (y=114.4) at 5 and 10 mg/L - below the 10-min gridline, while the control point sits above it, so the gridline itself separates them and the 6.6 px gap is easy. The other three never go below their lowest plotted values of 21 (J, at 20 mg/L), 21 (K, at 5 mg/L) and 16 (M, at 5 mg/L), all well above 12. No second option is defensible. CAVEAT: the 0 mg/L point is NOT labelled 'no additive' anywhere in the drawing - it is an unlabelled open circle of a fifth marker shape that appears in no legend, and the only thing identifying it as the control is the passage sentence 'their mean is plotted at 0 mg/L'. That is legitimate (ACT expects the passage to be read) and it is what makes the item more than a lookup, but it does mean a student working from the figure alone cannot solve it. I would add a short 'no additive' annotation or leave it exactly as is deliberately - not accidentally. Distractors plausible rather than strong: all three wrong additives fail for the SAME single reason (never below 12), so they are interchangeable and a student who locates the control line eliminates all three in one move; there is no graded near-miss the way Q2 has M. Author called this hard; the passage sentence is explicit and the visual gap is large, so medium.

_batch_note.figure_reconstruction: CHECKED INDEPENDENTLY, and the author's claim holds. I decoded both panels from the raw SVG coordinates and separately rendered the SVG at the authored width=340 and read it by eye; the two agree on all 24 points. Figure 1: y=132 is 0, y=22 is 50, 2.2 px/min; x at 45/116/187/258/329 is 0/5/10/15/20 mg/L. J 12,30,44,36,21 (solid, filled circles). K 12,21,27,29,30 (long dash, open squares). L 12,9,8,18,36 (dotted, filled triangles). M 12,16,40,42,41 (dash-dot, open diamonds). All four share the 12-min control point at 0 mg/L. Every plotted marker centre lands on its own polyline vertex, and every right-edge letter sits beside the correct line end. Figure 2: y=234 is 0, y=174 is 50, 1.2 px/min. Unstirred/stirred = J 44/17, K 27/29, L 8/7, M 40/36. THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE the figure is sound: Figure 2's four unstirred bars equal Figure 1's four values at 10 mg/L exactly (44, 27, 8, 40), which is what the shared protocol requires and which nothing in the authoring process forced - two independently drawn panels agreeing on their one shared condition. Nothing in either panel contradicts the passage or an explanation.
_batch_note.ticks_and_markers_i_found_hard_to_resolv: Three, in order of severity. (1) Figure 2 is gridded and labelled ONLY at 0, 25 and 50 min, so every within-pair comparison is made against 25-min reference intervals. K's +2 min key margin in Q3 is 2.4 px and L's -1 min is 1.2 px at the authored size; both are below what that axis supports, and at first glance at 340 px the K pair reads as a tie. This is the batch's one real weakness. (2) Additive M's top three points in Figure 1 (40, 42, 41 at 10, 15, 20 mg/L) span 4.4 px total and form a near-plateau; Q2 depends on the student seeing 42 > 40. The 40-min gridline passing exactly through the 10 mg/L diamond is what makes it readable, which is luck of placement rather than design. (3) K's open square (3.6 px) versus M's open diamond (4.4 px) is the finest symbol distinction, but the dash patterns and right-edge letters make curve identity redundant, so this one never bit. Minor Figure 1 tick note: the axis carries minor tick marks at the 5-min lines (y=121, 99, 77, 55, 33) but no minor gridlines and no labels, so odd values are read by halving a gridline interval - fine, and consistent with real ACT figures.
_batch_note.cross_item_guessability: Structurally this batch is the cleanest kind for the leakage rule in CLAUDE.md - ask whether the OPTION SET alone can decide the item, and here it cannot, for all six. Q2, Q3 and Q6 offer nothing but the four additive labels (in Q2, four identical sentences differing by one letter), which carry no propositional content at all; Q1, Q4 and Q5 offer four bare minute values, meaningless until the stem says what they measure - the same reason the numeric-maths stratum measures clean. There is no hedged-key tell, no length tell (options are near-identical in length within every item), and no speech-act asymmetry to exploit. Key slots are B, D, A, D, C, A - spread 2/1/1/2 across A-D with no run and no dominant slot, and this survives the 4-item-group permutation tell too (no group of four here is a complete ABCD cycle). TWO PATTERNS I WOULD STILL RECORD. First, a mild round-robin: the six keys reference M, J, K, J, K, L, so all four additives appear and each of the three additive-named items (Q2, Q3, Q6) keys to a DIFFERENT additive, with Q1 spending the fourth. A student who has answered Q1 (M), Q2 (J) and Q3 (K) and assumes the set gives each additive a turn arrives at L for Q6 without looking - which is the correct answer. With six items this is weak, and every item still demands real figure work, but it is exactly the 'answer predictable from the brief rather than the content' shape that reached the bank three times before; when this passage grows to the full 25MC5 shape, deliberately repeat an additive as the key of two label-option items. Second, the off-curve-value point logged under Q5. Neither is a leak today; both are templates that would become leaks if the next batch is authored to the same spec.
_batch_note.overall: Six for six on my own solve, all matching the stated keys; no item dropped. The passage is self-consistent, the two panels are mutually consistent on their shared condition, and Q4 is a genuinely well-built hard item. The one thing I would change before a human sitting is Figure 2's axis: label and grid it every 10 min, or widen K's stirred-versus-unstirred margin. Q3's key currently rests on a 2.4 px difference and survives my exclusivity test only because the alternative misread produces a tie rather than a rival answer - which is a thinner margin than a shipped item should run on.
